books.section: Topic 4.2 The Rise of Political Parties and the Era of Jefferson, B. The Supreme Court Asserts Federal Power and the Power of the Judiciary

stimulus.source_note: Chief Justice John Marshall, McCulloch v. Maryland (1819), public domain. Abridged. The Gibbons sentence is a paraphrase of the decision, labeled as such.
stimulus.text:
“That the power to tax involves the power to destroy; that the power to destroy may defeat and render useless the power to create.”
— Chief Justice John Marshall, McCulloch v. Maryland, 1819 (abridged)

[Paraphrase: In Gibbons v. Ogden (1824) the Court ruled that only Congress could regulate trade between the states, and struck down New York's grant of a steamboat monopoly on waters between New York and New Jersey.]

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim public-domain excerpt from McCulloch v. Maryland (1819) plus a labeled paraphrase of Gibbons v. Ogden
stem: In McCulloch v. Maryland, the Court ruled that

options.text: Congress could charter the Second Bank, and Maryland could not tax it
Maryland could tax the Second Bank because states control banks in their borders
options.misconception: Marshall ruled the opposite: a state tax on a federal institution was unconstitutional.

options.text: Congress had no power to charter a bank, since the Constitution never names one
options.misconception: The Court upheld the bank under the Necessary and Proper Clause, reading Congress's powers broadly.

options.text: the Supreme Court could not hear cases about state taxes
options.misconception: The Court heard the case and decided it; it also affirmed in Cohens v. Virginia that it could hear appeals from state courts.

rationales.A: Marshall upheld the Second Bank as a proper means for Congress to carry out its listed powers, and held Maryland's tax on it unconstitutional, because the power to tax involves the power to destroy. A state could not tax a federal institution out of existence. Background: the decision read the Necessary and Proper Clause broadly, the loose construction Jefferson had always opposed.
rationales.B: Marshall ruled the opposite: a state tax on a federal institution was unconstitutional.
rationales.C: The Court upheld the bank under the Necessary and Proper Clause, reading Congress's powers broadly.
rationales.D: The Court heard the case and decided it. It also affirmed in Cohens v. Virginia that it could hear appeals from state courts.
rationales.general:
1. Read the warning. The power to tax involves the power to destroy.
2. Ask who is taxing whom. Maryland is taxing the Second Bank, a federal institution.
3. Ask what Marshall concludes. A state cannot tax a federal creation out of existence.
4. Put it together. The bank stands because federal power stands above state interference.
Remember: when a state taxes a federal thing, ask whether the tax is really a veto.
